card.title: How sites can store passwords safely

body.claim: A safer way for a site to store passwords is as salted hashes, not as the passwords themselves.
body.why: A hash is a one-way operation that is quick to calculate but hard to reverse, and even a small change in the input gives a very different result. A salt is random data added to each password, which helps defend against precomputed tables like rainbow tables.

probes.question: What does adding a unique salt to each password help defend against?
options: Attacks using precomputed tables of hashes

probes.question: True or false: a hash is designed to be easy to reverse.

claims.claim: Safer to store salted hashes than the passwords themselves (plain text needs no cracking)
claims.quote: If an attacker gains access to the password file, then if it is stored as plain text, no cracking is necessary.

claims.claim: Hashed but unsalted passwords are vulnerable to rainbow tables, hence salting
claims.quote: If it is hashed but not salted then it is vulnerable to rainbow table attacks

claims.claim: A hash is one-way: quick to calculate, hard to reverse (probe 2: false)
claims.quote: Hashing is a one-directional mathematical operation which is quick to calculate, yet hard to reverse.

claims.claim: Even a small change in the input gives a very different hash
claims.quote: Even a small change in the input results in a very different hash

claims.claim: A salt is random data added to the password hashing
claims.quote: a salt is random data fed as an additional input to a one-way function that hashes data, a password or passphrase

claims.claim: A unique salt is generated for each password
claims.quote: Typically, a unique salt is randomly generated for each password.

claims.claim: Salting helps defend against precomputed tables like rainbow tables (probe 1)
claims.quote: Salting helps defend against attacks that use partially precomputed tables
